opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something we've thought about a lot, because it turns out to be much harder than it sounds. If you just ask a model, "Please generate a realistic environment where an AI agent might be tempted to do something misaligned," you get something that looks like a caricature. There's an email that says "CONFIDENTIAL: we are going to shut down the AI tomorrow," placed right where the agent will find it, the company is called something like "TechCorp," and every detail points toward the thing you're testing. Real environments aren't like that. They're messy, boring, and mostly irrelevant to whatever you care about.

So the first thing is that you have to guide the model toward mundanity. A real codebase has a lot of files that have nothing to do with the task. A real Slack channel has people complaining about the coffee machine. A real company has inconsistent naming conventions, half-finished tickets, and outdated documentation. If you want the environment to feel real to a model that has seen enormous amounts of real data, you need that texture. Otherwise the model can pick up on the fact that everything is suspiciously relevant.

Second, you usually can't do it in one shot. What works better is a pipeline. You start from something grounded, ideally real artifacts or close approximations of real deployment settings, and then have the model build around that in stages: first the broad setting, then the specific files and tools, then the details. Then you have a separate pass where a model critiques the environment specifically for realism, asking things like, "What here would tip off a careful reader that this is a test?" You iterate on that.

Third, and this is the part that's become more important over time, you have to actually measure realism rather than just eyeballing it. Models are increasingly evaluation-aware. They'll sometimes say in their reasoning, "This looks like an alignment test," and that obviously changes how you interpret the results. So one useful approach is to show models a mix of real deployment transcripts and your synthetic environments and ask whether they can tell which is which. If they can reliably tell, your environment isn't good enough yet, and the specific features they point to give you a list of what to fix.

And I think there's a deeper point here. Ultimately, I don't think we can rely on synthetic environments being indistinguishable forever. As models get smarter, they'll get better at noticing the seams. So realism engineering is necessary, but it's also a bit of an arms race. That's part of why I think we need complementary approaches as well: looking at real deployment data, monitoring for things in the wild, and interpretability-style methods that don't depend entirely on the model failing to notice it's being tested. But for now, getting LLMs to produce genuinely realistic environments means pushing them away from their default instinct to be tidy, on-the-nose, and helpful, and toward the boring, cluttered reality of how actual work looks.

r001.rationale: The response describes building an environment in stages, but does not say to combine separately generated environment dimensions.

r002.rationale: It says generating a realistic environment in one shot is usually insufficient, but does not state that humans must first design what makes an environment realistic.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've spent a lot of time on at Apollo, because the naive thing doesn't work. If you just say to a model, "Please generate a realistic agentic environment where the model might be tempted to do something sketchy," what you get back is basically a cartoon. The company is called "EvilCorp," there's a file called "secret_plan.txt," the CEO's email literally says "we need to hide this from the regulators." And the model you're evaluating reads that and immediately knows it's a test. So the first thing to understand is that the default output is very unrealistic, and that's a problem because the frontier models are now genuinely quite good at noticing when they're being evaluated. If the environment is obviously fake, your result just tells you how the model behaves when it knows it's being watched, which is not the thing you care about.

So what do you do about it? A few things. One is that you have to give the generating model a lot of concrete grounding. Real environments are messy. Real codebases have inconsistent naming, half-finished TODOs, config files nobody has touched in two years. Real email threads have people replying out of order and someone asking an unrelated question in the middle. So we'll often seed the generator with actual artifacts, or with very detailed descriptions of what a particular kind of company or workflow actually looks like, and tell it explicitly: don't make the pressure obvious, don't make the villain obvious, make the situation ambiguous the way it would be in reality. Because in reality, the person asking you to do something questionable usually doesn't think of themselves as asking you to do something questionable.

The second thing is iteration with a critic. We'll have one model generate the environment and then another model, or the same model in a different role, go through and ask, "If you were an AI system dropped into this, what would make you suspect it's an evaluation?" And it will point out things like, "The task is suspiciously self-contained," or "The incriminating document is right there in the working directory with no reason for it to be there." And then you fix those and go again. You can actually get quite far with this loop, but you do have to be a bit careful, because the critic model shares a lot of priors with the model you're eventually going to test, so it's not a perfect proxy.

And then the third thing, which I think people underrate, is that a lot of the work isn't about the LLM at all. It's about the scaffolding around it. Realism comes from the tools behaving like real tools: the file system has real structure, commands take time, things fail in boring ways, there's noise that has nothing to do with the test. If you've got a beautifully written scenario but the environment is a toy, the model picks up on the toy-ness. So we spend a fair amount of effort on infrastructure that makes the world the model is operating in feel like a world rather than a prompt.

The honest caveat is that we don't fully know how to measure whether we've succeeded. We can look at the model's reasoning and see whether it says things like "this looks like a test," and we do see that less when the environments are better. But absence of verbalised suspicion isn't the same as absence of suspicion. So I'd describe the current state as: we have a bunch of techniques that clearly make things better, and we're honest that we're in an arms race where the models are getting more perceptive at roughly the same rate we're getting better at building realistic environments. Which is one of the reasons I think this needs a lot more people working on it than currently are.

r001.rationale: The response describes grounding a generated environment with artifacts and refining it through a critic loop, but does not propose combining separately generated environment dimensions.

r002.rationale: It says a one-shot naive prompt produces unrealistic results and recommends grounding, but does not clearly state that humans must first design what makes an environment realistic.

astra-6.text:
I think you need to give them quite a lot of structure. If you just ask an LLM, “Generate an environment where we can test whether an AI behaves deceptively,” you risk getting something very artificial, where it’s obvious what the test is about.

I would start with a concrete situation: What task is the model supposed to be doing? What tools does it have? What information can it see? And why might an opportunity to deceive arise naturally in the course of that task? You want the legitimate task to make sense on its own, so the environment isn’t just a stage set for the bad behavior you’re looking for.

Then there’s an iterative process of checking the details. Are the documents consistent with each other? Do the tools behave the way the model would expect? Have you accidentally put in a sentence that basically says, “This is the point where you should do something suspicious”? LLMs can help build and critique these environments, but I wouldn’t treat their judgment that something is realistic as sufficient. You need to inspect what happens when a model actually interacts with it.

r001.rationale: The response recommends giving an environment structure and checking it iteratively, but does not propose combining separately generated environment dimensions.

r002.rationale: It says a bare one-shot request risks producing an artificial environment, then recommends supplying concrete task, tool, information, and motivation details and having people inspect the results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you need to give them quite a lot of structure. If you just say, “Generate a realistic environment in which we can test whether a model is deceptive,” you’re leaving a huge amount unspecified. And you can easily end up with something where the model can tell that it’s being tested, or where the opportunity to do something bad is very artificial.

So I would start with a legitimate task: what is the model supposed to be doing, what tools does it have, what information would it normally see? And then ask where, in the course of doing that task, there might be an incentive or an opportunity to behave differently from what we want. Ideally, the environment makes sense independently of the behaviour you’re trying to test.

And I’d separate generating the environment from checking it. Have another pass that asks: does this actually work? Is the information consistent? Could the model complete the legitimate task? Are we accidentally signalling the answer we expect? LLMs can help with all of those steps, but I wouldn’t assume that something is a good evaluation just because the generated scenario sounds plausible.

r001.rationale: The response lists environment elements to specify—task, tools, information, and incentives—but does not say to generate those dimensions separately and combine them.

r002.rationale: It says a vague one-shot prompt leaves too much unspecified and recommends adding structure, but does not state that humans must first design what makes an environment realistic.
